$comment: The one source of truth for architectural style. src/city/facade.ts reads it to plan a facade; tools/facadegen/paint.py reads the same file to paint the atlas those plans point at. Ranges are [min, max] and are sampled per building from the building's own seed, so a street is varied but a building is stable.

styles.name: Haussmann
styles.note: Paris, 1860s. The most rule-bound facade ever built: stone courses line up down the whole street, continuous iron balconies on the second and fifth floors, a grey zinc mansard on top, shops at the pavement.

styles.name: Brownstone
styles.note: A New York or Boston row house. Narrow, raised over a basement, reached by a stoop, tall sash windows getting shorter as they go up, and a deep bracketed cornice at the roofline.

styles.name: Classical
styles.note: The nineteenth-century civic and commercial block: a rusticated base you can read from across the street, pilasters running up the middle floors, pediments over the good windows, and a heavy entablature closing it off.

styles.name: Brick
styles.note: The ordinary workhorse of every city: load-bearing brick, punched windows in a flat wall, soldier courses over the openings, a parapet with a stone coping instead of a cornice. Warehouse versions get big multi-pane industrial windows.

styles.name: Bauhaus
styles.note: Interwar modernism: white render, horizontal ribbon windows that turn the corner, flat roof, a thin steel railing, and nothing applied to the wall that is not doing a job.

styles.name: Brutalist
styles.note: Board-marked concrete, deep-set windows in a thick wall, floor slabs left showing as horizontal bands, and a module repeated without apology.

styles.name: Skyscraper
styles.note: A curtain wall: the building behind it is a frame, and what you see is glass and spandrel panel in a narrow repeating module, with setbacks and a crown instead of a cornice.

styles.name: Marais
styles.note: Paris before Haussmann: the 17th- and 18th-century streets of the Marais. Narrow plastered or rough-limestone fronts, tall shuttered casements, a small cornice, a steep slate roof with dormers, and a painted wooden shopfront at the pavement. Four or five storeys, lower and plainer than the boulevards.

styles.name: Tenement
styles.note: New York, 1880–1920: the five- and six-storey brick walk-up, shops at the pavement, a deep pressed-metal cornice, and the fire escape zig-zagging down the front — the building every New York street is made of.

styles.name: Chicago School
styles.note: Chicago, 1885–1910: the first skyscrapers — a steel frame dressed in terracotta, broad bays filled with the Chicago window (a wide fixed pane between two narrow sashes), piers running up the whole height, and a deep projecting cornice.

styles.name: Victorian
styles.note: San Francisco, 1870–1905: narrow timber row houses on seven-metre lots, a bay window through every storey of the front, a gable or a false front, a stair up to a raised ground floor, and three-colour paint.

styles.name: Place des Vosges
styles.note: Henri IV's square, 1605–1612, and never used anywhere else in the city: red brick dressed with white stone — each window in a stone frame, the frames joined floor to floor into vertical stone chains — over a continuous stone arcade, under steep slate roofs. Given only by the landmark manifest's restyle, never chosen by the bake.

styles.name: Opéra Bastille
styles.note: Carlos Ott, 1989: pale grey granite in a square grid framing square panels of blue-grey glass, flat roofs, no cornice to speak of. Given only by the landmark manifest's restyle.

styles.name: Opéra Bastille (glass)
styles.note: The Opéra's curved front: stepped tiers of pale silvery glass in a fine grid, over the dark recessed ground floor — the other half of its black-and-white look. Given only by the Opéra's restyle, to the parts that start above the ground.

styles.name: Marina stucco
styles.note: San Francisco, 1925–1940: the Marina and Cow Hollow rebuilt after 1915 — smooth pale stucco in cream, peach and mint, arched windows, a garage in the ground storey with the front door up a short stair beside it, a flat parapet with a tiled coping. Mediterranean and Art Deco, two or three storeys.

styles.name: SF apartment
styles.note: San Francisco, 1906–1930: the Edwardian and 1920s apartment block that fills Nob Hill, Russian Hill, the Tenderloin and Pacific Heights — four to seven storeys of stucco or buff brick, bay windows in stacks up the front, a fire escape, a deep cornice, the entrance in a recess.

styles.name: Chinatown
styles.note: San Francisco's Chinatown, rebuilt after 1906: three- to five-storey brick and stucco walk-ups painted in strong colours, iron balconies across the upper floors, shops and restaurants below under signs, and on the family-association buildings a green-tiled eave and red trim.

styles.name: Edwardian
styles.note: San Francisco, 1906–1924: the flats and houses that rebuilt the city after the fire — two and three storeys on the 25-foot lot, a boxy bay through the upper floors, a flat roof behind a bracketed, dentilled cornice rather than a gable, clapboard or stucco in muted colours, and a garage cut into the ground storey since.

styles.name: apartment tower
styles.note: The post-war residential tower: twelve to thirty-five storeys of pale concrete or stucco with punched windows, a flat top and no cornice. San Francisco's hill crests are full of them (Russian Hill, Nob Hill, Cathedral Hill, the Marina), and before this style existed they were all inferred as glass office towers, which is the wrong city entirely.

styles.name: Presidio clapboard
styles.note: The Army's frame buildings (owner, 2026-10-17: 'in the presidio area, buildings are unique bright white clapboard with red roofs, OR brick with red roofs'): the Funston Avenue officers' row, Letterman's wards on O'Reilly, the Simonds Loop and Ruger Street cottages, Fort Baker's parade ground, Upper Fort Mason. Painted lap siding in BRIGHT white (the old smooth cream render read as stone), white casings and corner boards, six-over-six sash, a door under a little porch now and then, a red roof (tools/bake.ts roofFor: gabled, a moderate pitch). Mapillary 6339758482786544 (Funston), 526567306262392 (O'Reilly), 589332340043537 (Simonds); Commons 'Fort Baker (Sausalito, CA).jpg'. One to three storeys.

styles.name: Presidio brick
styles.note: The Army's brick (owner, 2026-10-17: 'Housing on Liggett Ave near the Presidio are all uniform brick … brick with red roofs'): the EAST HOUSING round Liggett, Clarke, Sanches and Portola (1930s Georgian Revival duplexes — Mapillary 797055755405312, 237668289059428, 3500112376932569), the Main Post's Montgomery Street barracks and Riley Avenue NCO duplexes (306302501733129, 1073064896995947), the Hardie/Barnard barracks and Fort Scott's Wright Loop (1255041638546569, 809997674114962). Orange-red common brick, white six-over-six sash in white frames under a flat white lintel, a white entry portico, a RED roof — red-brown weathered tile in East Housing, a brighter red at the Main Post (the palettes carry both). Two or three storeys.

styles.name: Presidio Mission stucco
styles.note: The Army's Mission Revival (Presidio research, 2026-10-17): FORT WINFIELD SCOTT's barracks and officers' rows round its parade ground (Mapillary 1298821577386783 Ralston, 1359139001338251 Upton, 1324647778487839 Greenough, 1419593392151266 Pilots' Row), the Amatury Loop housing (1349986875932665), Golden Gate Park's lodges and Lower Fort Mason's sheds: smooth white-to-cream stucco, deep-set sash with no lintel, an arched door, a low-pitched red clay-tile roof (tools/bake.ts roofFor). One to three storeys.

styles.name: Cape Cod shingle
styles.note: Sausalito's houses (owner, 2026-10-06: 'much more cape cod style and modern style'): weathered cedar shingle, crisp white trim and sash windows, a steep gabled roof in grey shingle. One to three storeys.

styles.name: Fisherman's Wharf
styles.note: San Francisco's Fisherman's Wharf (owner, 2026-10-16: 'the feel of Fisherman's Wharf … does NOT need to be a perfect copy'): two- and three-storey restaurants and shops along Jefferson, Beach and Taylor, painted timber in sea-weathered white, pale blue, sea green, butter yellow and barn red, with the odd 1900s brick-red front. Big glazed shopfronts under striped canvas, fascia boards lettered SEAFOOD, CRAB, CHOWDER, GIFTS in bold poster letters, a life-ring or a ship's wheel by the sign; plain sash windows above under a simple cornice.

styles.name: SF shop-and-flats
styles.note: San Francisco, 1880-1925: the Mission's and Valencia's and Castro's commercial street building — two or three storeys of timber or stucco flats over a row of shops, bay windows up the front, a bracketed cornice or false front. Drawn with the Victorian's windows and clapboard over the generic storefronts (`art`, `groundArt`: no new painting). Owner, 2026-10-21: the Mission was SoMa's brick lofts.

styles.name: SF storefront
styles.note: San Francisco, 1920-1970: the one- and two-storey shop building of every neighbourhood street — plain stucco or block over a glazed shop, a tall parapet carrying the sign. Drawn with the Presidio stucco's sash windows and render over the generic storefronts (`art`, `groundArt`).

styles.name: SF apartment hotel
styles.note: San Francisco, 1906-1930: the Beaux-Arts apartment hotel of Lower Nob Hill and the Tenderloin — cream or buff terracotta and stucco, a rusticated base round an arched central entry, a heavy bracketed cornice, often a fire escape down the front (owner's photographs, 2026-10-21). Drawn with the Classical style's windows, stone and arched entry (`art`).

styles.name: SF brick apartments
styles.note: San Francisco, 1906-1930: the brick apartment hotel — red, brown or buff brick with cream terracotta trim, sash windows in a flat front, fire escapes zig-zagging down it, a bracketed cornice; the 'tenement' look of the Tenderloin and Nob Hill (owner's photographs, 2026-10-21). Drawn with the Tenement's brick and windows over an arched entry (`art`).

styles.name: SF Mediterranean apartments
styles.note: San Francisco, 1920-1940: the Mediterranean, Spanish and Deco apartment block of the Marina, Pacific Heights and Russian Hill — white, cream or salmon stucco, arched windows, wrought-iron balconettes, a parapet or a tiled coping, the garage and the entry at the pavement (owner's photographs, 2026-10-21). Drawn with the Marina stucco's windows, render and garage (`art`).

styles.name: SF modern apartments
styles.note: San Francisco, 1955 on: the cheap modern block — a box of render or panels, aluminium windows, balconies or none, garages under, and bright colour blocks laid over groups of bays (owner, 2026-10-21: 'cheap modern buildings all are boxy and bright colored'). Drawn with the Bauhaus ribbon windows over the stucco garage (`art`).

styles.name: SF contemporary apartments
styles.note: San Francisco, 1990 on: the better modern block — white render, charcoal panel or warm timber, glass, box bays standing out of the front, glass balconies, a roof slab overhanging (owner, 2026-10-21: 'modern buildings have even more variety, especially nicer ones'). Drawn with the Bauhaus ribbon glass over a glazed base (`art`).

styles.name: SF stucco flats
styles.note: San Francisco, 1915-1960: the two- and three-storey flats and houses the edwardian proportions built in smooth stucco rather than clapboard - the commonest ordinary front in the Sunset, Richmond and Mission (appearance research, 2026-10-22: a label saying stucco must not be drawn as wood siding). Drawn with the Presidio stucco's sash windows and render, and the Marina's garage (`art`, `groundArt`; wave 6: the Marina's arched windows went on every plain stucco front).

styles.name: SF stucco shop-and-flats
styles.note: The shop-and-flats in smooth stucco: two to four storeys of rendered flats over a row of shops - Mission and Geary Boulevard. Drawn with the Marina stucco's windows and render over the generic storefronts (`art`, `groundArt`).
